title: Steam Takes to Water and Road
summary: A French army engineer built a huge, wobbly steam wagon, and inventors in France, America and Scotland tried putting engines in boats. Soon steamboats chugged up rivers, giant iron ships crossed oceans, steam tractors ploughed fields and a steam car zoomed faster than 200 kilometres an hour. Steam was on the move!

sections.heading: Cugnot's Monster on Three Wheels
paragraphs: Imagine standing in a courtyard in Paris around 1770. In front of you is something nobody has ever seen: a heavy wooden cart with one wheel at the front and two at the back. Hanging out in front of that single front wheel is a big, round copper boiler, hissing and steaming like an enormous kettle. Two brass cylinders, pumping up and down, turn the front wheel. There are no horses. The machine creaks forward at about walking pace, and the crowd gasps.

This was the 'fardier à vapeur', which means 'steam wagon' (a fardier was a heavy cart for hauling big loads). It was built by Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot, a French military engineer born in 1725 in Lorraine. The French army wanted a way to drag heavy cannons without needing teams of horses, which had to be fed, watered and rested. Cugnot tested a small version in 1769, and the full-size machine was built in 1770.

The fardier was a beast. Empty, it weighed about 2.5 tonnes. It was meant to carry around 4 tonnes and travel at almost 8 kilometres an hour, but it never managed that. The best reports suggest it crawled along at a few kilometres an hour. Its biggest problem was its boiler. It had no separate firebox that could be kept going easily, so every quarter of an hour or so the machine had to stop, relight or rebuild the fire, and wait for the pressure to rise again before it could move on.

It was also very hard to control. Because the heavy boiler hung out in front of the single steering wheel, the whole weight sat over the front, and the machine was clumsy to steer and unstable. A famous story says that in 1771 it crashed into a wall, making it the world's first motor accident. But be careful with this tale: no report from the time mentions the crash, and it first appears in writing around 1804, more than thirty years later. It may have happened, or it may be a legend that grew with retelling.

Whatever the truth, the army lost interest, and the project was put away. Cugnot's machine survived, though, and in 1800 it was moved to the Conservatoire national des arts et métiers in Paris, a museum of science and technology, where you can still see it today. It is one of the oldest surviving self-propelled vehicles in the world. In 2010, engineering students in France built a working copy, which was shown at the Paris Motor Show.

Cugnot's wagon was too early. Engines in 1770 were heavy, low-pressure and wasteful, and roads were rutted and rough. But he had proved one huge thing: a fire could make a vehicle move by itself. The next inventors would find that steam was much happier first on water, where a boat could carry a heavy engine without sinking into the mud.

sections.heading: Paddles on French and American Rivers
paragraphs: Why put an engine in a boat? For thousands of years, boats had been moved by oars, sails, river currents, or horses walking along a towpath pulling them by rope. Going downstream was easy. Going upstream against a strong current, or across a lake with no wind, was slow and hard. An engine that never got tired, and did not care which way the wind blew, could change all that.

One of the first to try was a French nobleman, Claude de Jouffroy d'Abbans. In 1774, he built a boat called the Palmipède, a word meaning 'web-footed', because it tried to copy a duck's feet with flapping paddles driven by steam. It did not work well. So he tried again. On 15 July 1783, his new boat, the Pyroscaphe (from Greek words meaning 'fire boat'), steamed on the River Saône in eastern France. It was about 13 metres long, and instead of flapping oars it used paddle wheels turned by a steam engine. It made several trips up and down the river, pushing against the current. This was one of the first times a steam engine had driven a boat in a real trial.

Sadly for Jouffroy, he could not win official approval and money to build more, and a few years later the French Revolution turned his world upside down. His invention faded, but he is remembered in France as a steamboat pioneer.

Across the Atlantic, in the newly independent United States, two inventors were racing each other. John Fitch, born in Connecticut in 1743, was a clockmaker, silversmith and surveyor with almost no money but enormous determination. On 22 August 1787, his steamboat Perseverance made a successful run on the Delaware River at Philadelphia. Watching were delegates to the Constitutional Convention, the meeting that was writing the United States Constitution that very summer. Fitch's boat did not use paddle wheels. Instead, the engine worked rows of oars on each side, dipping and pulling like a team of rowers.

In 1790, Fitch built a 60-foot (about 18-metre) boat with steam-driven oars at the stern, and ran a real passenger service on the Delaware between Philadelphia and Burlington, New Jersey, carrying up to 30 passengers at about 6 to 8 miles an hour (roughly 10 to 13 kilometres an hour). That is pretty impressive for 1790! But there were too few customers, the service lost money, and investors gave up.

Fitch's rival was James Rumsey of Virginia, who in December 1787 demonstrated a boat on the Potomac River that used a steam pump to suck water in at the front and squirt it out of the back, a kind of early water-jet. The two men argued bitterly over who deserved the credit. In 1791, the new United States patent office gave Fitch a patent, but it also gave steamboat patents to Rumsey and others on the same day, so Fitch never got the monopoly he hoped for. He died in 1798, poor and disappointed. A steamboat needed more than a working engine. It needed money, the right river, enough customers and good timing.

sections.heading: Scotland's Canal Tug and the Comet
paragraphs: Meanwhile, in Scotland, a young engineer named William Symington was working on the same dream. In 1788, he and a wealthy banker named Patrick Miller tried a small steam-driven paddle boat on Dalswinton Loch, a lake on Miller's estate. It worked, but Miller lost interest after further trials, and the work stalled.

Symington's chance came again when Lord Dundas, the governor of the Forth and Clyde Canal Company, backed him. Canal boats were usually pulled by horses walking along the bank, and a powerful steam tug could, in theory, haul many boats at once. A first boat was tried in 1801. Then, in 1803, Symington built a new and better one, named the Charlotte Dundas after Lord Dundas's daughter.

The Charlotte Dundas was about 17 metres (56 feet) long, with a horizontal steam engine turning a single big paddle wheel set inside the stern, so its splashing would not hit the canal banks. In its famous trial in 1803, in a strong headwind that stopped other boats, it towed two loaded barges, each weighing about 70 tons, for roughly 30 kilometres (about 19 miles) along the canal to Glasgow. The trip took about nine and a quarter hours, which may sound slow, but no other boat could have done it against that wind.

Yet the canal owners said no. They feared that the waves from the paddle wheel would wash away the soft canal banks. The Charlotte Dundas was left in a quiet backwater, where it slowly rotted until it was broken up in 1861. Many people consider it the first practical steamboat, because it did a real job well, even though it never went into regular service.

Scotland did get its working steamboat soon after. In 1812, Henry Bell launched the Comet, which carried passengers on the River Clyde between Glasgow and Greenock (the town where James Watt was born). It is usually counted as the first commercially successful passenger steamboat service in Europe. Before long, dozens of little steamers were puffing up and down the Clyde, and Glasgow became one of the greatest shipbuilding cities in the world.

sections.heading: Fulton's Boat on the Hudson
paragraphs: Robert Fulton is often called the inventor of the steamboat, but as you have just seen, that is not true. Jouffroy, Fitch, Rumsey and Symington had all made steamboats move before him. Fulton's achievement was different and just as important: he was the first to make a steamboat service that worked as a business, year after year.

Fulton was born in Pennsylvania in 1765 and started out as a painter of miniature portraits. He moved to Europe, became fascinated by canals and engineering, and in 1803 tested a small steamboat on the River Seine in Paris. There he teamed up with Robert Livingston, a rich and powerful American who was then serving as the United States minister (ambassador) to France. Livingston held something very valuable: a legal monopoly from the state of New York, which gave him the sole right to run steamboats on New York's waters, as long as he could produce a working boat.

Back in New York, the partners had a boat built at the Charles Browne shipyard. Its engine was ordered from Boulton & Watt in Birmingham, England, and shipped across the Atlantic. The boat was long and narrow, with a paddle wheel on each side and a tall smokestack. People called it the North River Steamboat, because the Hudson River was then often called the North River.

On 17 August 1807, the boat set off from New York City for Albany, the state capital, about 150 miles (240 kilometres) up the Hudson. Some onlookers expected it to fail or blow up. Instead, it puffed steadily upstream against the current at an average of about 5 miles an hour (8 kilometres an hour). The trip took about 32 hours of travel, plus a stop of about 20 hours at Clermont, Livingston's family estate along the river. Sailing sloops, which depended on the wind, often took several days for the same journey. The return trip to New York took about 30 hours, with only a one-hour stop.

Regular passenger service began on 4 September 1807, with stops along the river. The boat was later widened and rebuilt to about 43 metres (142 feet) long. Many people today call it the Clermont, after Livingston's estate, but that name was not used at the time. It first appeared in a biography of Fulton written in 1817, two years after his death, and it simply stuck.

Fulton's success opened the floodgates. In 1811, a steamboat named New Orleans, built by Fulton and Livingston's partners, set off down the Ohio and Mississippi rivers, the start of the great age of Mississippi riverboats. Within a few decades, hundreds of steamboats were carrying cotton, grain, timber and passengers up and down America's rivers, helping cities like St. Louis and Cincinnati to grow. Because they could travel upstream as easily as down, steamboats turned rivers into two-way highways. They also brought new dangers, especially boiler explosions, which we will look at in the next part.

sections.heading: Steaming Across the Ocean
paragraphs: Rivers and canals were one thing. The Atlantic Ocean, nearly 5,000 kilometres of wild water between Europe and North America, was quite another. A ship would need to carry enough coal for the whole trip, and early engines gobbled coal so fast that many experts thought it was impossible.

The first attempt was the American ship SS Savannah. In 1819 it sailed from Savannah, Georgia, to Liverpool, England, in 29 days and 11 hours. But it was really a sailing ship with a steam engine added. Its paddle wheels could even be folded up and stored on deck in about 15 minutes, so they did not drag in the water while the ship sailed. During the crossing, the engine ran for only about 80 hours, roughly a tenth of the voyage, because the ship could not carry more fuel. No passengers dared to buy a ticket, so the voyage was purely an experiment. Still, it was the first time a steam-powered ship had crossed the Atlantic, even partly under steam.

The real race came in 1838. A famous young English engineer, Isambard Kingdom Brunel, had already built the Great Western Railway from London to Bristol. According to a well-known story, he joked that it should simply continue all the way to New York, and he designed a big wooden paddle steamer to do it, also called the Great Western. Brunel understood something clever: if you build a ship twice as long, its cargo space grows much more than the push of water against it, so a really big ship can carry enough coal for an ocean crossing.

Rivals were determined to get there first. They chartered a smaller steamer called Sirius, which left before the Great Western and reached New York on 22 April 1838, almost out of coal. The Great Western, delayed by a fire in its engine room on its first trip, left Bristol on 8 April and arrived the very next day, 23 April, after a crossing of about 15 days, with around 200 tons of coal still in its bunkers. Sirius had won the race, but the Great Western had proved Brunel right: a well-designed ship could cross the Atlantic by steam with fuel to spare. Two years later, in 1840, Samuel Cunard's company began a regular steamship mail service across the Atlantic with its ship Britannia, and Atlantic steamship lines grew rapidly.

Brunel's next ship was a giant leap. The SS Great Britain, floated out at Bristol on 19 July 1843, was about 98 metres (322 feet) long, far larger than any ship before it. It combined two brand-new ideas for an ocean liner: a hull made of iron instead of wood, and a screw propeller instead of paddle wheels. In 1845 it became the first iron-hulled steamship to cross the Atlantic, taking just under 15 days.

Why a propeller? Paddle wheels work by slapping water backwards with flat boards, like someone rowing. They work well on calm rivers, but on the open ocean a ship rolls from side to side, so one paddle wheel lifts out of the water while the other plunges deep, and the ship lurches. Paddle wheels are also big and easy targets in a war. A screw propeller is a set of twisted blades under the back of the ship. As it turns, it pushes water backwards, a bit like a fan or a screw twisting into wood, and it stays underwater whatever the waves are doing.

Not everyone was convinced, so the Royal Navy held a contest. On 3 April 1845, two ships with similar engines, the propeller-driven HMS Rattler and the paddle-driven HMS Alecto, were tied stern to stern and set off in opposite directions in a nautical tug of war. Rattler dragged Alecto backwards at about 2.8 knots. The propeller had won, and navies and shipping lines gradually switched to screws.

The SS Great Britain had an adventurous life. It ran aground in Dundrum Bay in Ireland in 1846, then later carried thousands of emigrants to Australia. It ended up abandoned in the Falkland Islands, before being towed home to Bristol in 1970. Today it sits in the very dry dock where it was built, as a museum ship you can walk through. Brunel went on to design an even bigger ship, the Great Eastern of 1858, about 211 metres long, which later laid the first lasting telegraph cable across the Atlantic in 1866.

sections.heading: Steam on Roads and Farms
paragraphs: While ships were conquering oceans, inventors had not forgotten Cugnot's dream of steam on the roads. In Britain in the 1820s and 1830s, engineers such as Goldsworthy Gurney and Walter Hancock built steam carriages and steam buses that carried paying passengers. In 1831, for example, Gurney's steam carriages ran a service between Gloucester and Cheltenham for several months. But many people disliked these noisy, smoky machines. Some turnpike trusts, which ran the toll roads, charged steam carriages huge tolls, and the railways soon offered faster, smoother journeys. The steam-carriage boom faded.

Steam on the roads found its real home in slow, heavy, powerful work. From about the 1850s, makers built 'traction engines': steam tractors with a boiler, a firebox and a big flywheel, two huge driving wheels at the back and two smaller steering wheels at the front. Before that, many farms had 'portable engines', which had wheels but had to be pulled from place to place by horses. A traction engine could drive itself.

On the farm, a traction engine could drive a threshing machine with a long leather belt from its flywheel, separating grain from straw far faster than people with flails. On the road, bigger 'road locomotives' hauled heavy loads such as timber, stone and giant boilers. Travelling fairs used gleaming 'showman's engines', painted in bright colours with twisted brass poles, to haul rides from town to town and then make electricity to light the fair at night.

The law did not make life easy for them. Britain's Locomotive Act of 1865, often called the 'Red Flag Act', limited road steam engines to 4 miles an hour in the country and 2 miles an hour in towns, with a crew of three, one of whom had to walk at least 60 yards ahead carrying a red flag to warn horse riders and carriages. In 1878 the red flag itself stopped being compulsory, though someone still had to walk about 20 yards ahead, and the low speed limits stayed for years.

Ploughing was one of steam's cleverest farm jobs. A heavy engine driving across soft, wet fields would sink in and squash the soil. So in the 1850s, the engineer John Fowler and others developed cable ploughing. Two engines stood at opposite edges of the field, each with a big winding drum underneath and a long steel wire rope. One engine wound in its rope, pulling a special 'balance plough' across the field, while the other paid out its rope. Then they swapped, pulling the plough back again, and the drivers signalled each other with toots on their whistles. Around the time of the First World War, Britain had a little over 600 pairs of ploughing engines at work.

Steam also helped build better roads. In 1867, the Kent company Aveling and Porter produced one of the first successful steamrollers, with a wide, heavy roller at the front instead of wheels. It was tested on roads in Chatham and Rochester and in Hyde Park in London. Steamrollers pressed down crushed stone and, later, hot tar, to make smooth, hard road surfaces, and some were still working in Britain in the 1950s. That is where our word 'steamroller' comes from, meaning to crush any opposition.

By the 1920s and 1930s, lighter and cheaper petrol and diesel tractors and lorries were taking over. The last new British traction engine was sold in 1944. But many were saved by enthusiasts. In 2016, a register listed 2,851 surviving self-moving steam engines in Britain and Ireland, and you can see them puffing proudly at steam rallies every summer.

And of course, the most famous steam vehicles of all ran on iron rails. From the early 1800s, steam locomotives began to pull trains, and within a few decades railways had changed travel, trade and even the way clocks were set. That is a huge story of its own, told in the separate Railways Deep Dive, so we will wave to the trains as they pass and stay on the road.

sections.heading: The Stanley Steamer and the Rocket
paragraphs: At the end of the 1800s, a new kind of road vehicle appeared: the motor car. Today we think of cars as running on petrol or electricity, but in the early days, steam was a serious rival. In 1902, of 909 new cars registered in the United States in one count, 485, more than half, were steam cars.

The most famous steam cars were made by identical twins, Francis E. Stanley and Freelan O. Stanley, from Maine. They had made a fortune making photographic plates, which they sold to Eastman Kodak. In 1897 they built their first car. In 1899, Freelan and his wife Flora drove a Stanley to the top of Mount Washington in New Hampshire, the highest mountain in the northeastern United States, the first car to climb its carriage road. Their company, the Stanley Motor Carriage Company, was formed in 1902.

A Stanley Steamer had a compact boiler, usually under the bonnet, heated by a burner that burned kerosene or petrol. The steam drove a small two-cylinder engine connected almost directly to the rear axle. There was no gearbox and no clutch. Steam cars were smooth, quiet and very strong when starting off, because steam pushes hardest when the engine is barely moving.

In 1906, the Stanleys built a special racing car, a long, low, streamlined machine shaped a bit like an upside-down boat, later nicknamed the Stanley Rocket. On the hard, flat sands of Ormond Beach, Florida, near Daytona, their driver Fred Marriott roared through a measured mile in 28.2 seconds, a speed of about 127.7 miles an hour (about 205 kilometres an hour). It was the fastest anyone on Earth had ever travelled in a car. The next year, Marriott tried to go even faster in an improved version, but the car hit a bump at a very high speed, flew into the air and broke apart. Marriott was hurt but survived, and never tried for the record again.

Remarkably, his steam-car record lasted more than a century. It was not until August 2009 that a British team, with Charles Burnett III driving their steam car 'Inspiration', beat it in California, at an average of about 139.8 miles an hour (about 225 kilometres an hour).

So why did steam cars disappear? A steam car had to heat its boiler before it could move, which took several minutes from cold, and it had to carry plenty of water and stop to refill often. Meanwhile, petrol cars got much better. The electric starter motor meant drivers no longer had to crank the engine by hand, and Henry Ford's assembly line made petrol cars like the Model T cheap enough for ordinary families. The Stanley company made its peak of 784 cars in 1908 and about 10,910 in total, but it closed in 1924. The American Doble company built brilliant steam cars that could start from cold in under a minute, but they were very expensive, and Doble stopped making cars in 1930.

In about 150 years, steam had gone from Cugnot's wobbly cannon wagon to ocean liners, farm giants and a car that could beat 200 kilometres an hour. It had shrunk the oceans, opened up rivers and carried millions of people to new lives in new countries. But all this power came with a cost. Behind the speed and the shining brass were children in mills and mines, exploding boilers and smoke-blackened cities. In the next part, we will look honestly at the dark side of steam.

deepDive: Who deserves credit for the steamboat? This is one of history's classic arguments about 'firsts', and the answer depends on what you mean by 'first'. If you mean the first steam engine to move a boat in a public trial, the honour goes to Jouffroy d'Abbans's Pyroscaphe on the Saône in 1783. If you mean the first regular passenger service, John Fitch ran one on the Delaware in 1790, seventeen years before Fulton. If you mean the first steamboat to do a hard commercial job convincingly, many historians point to Symington's Charlotte Dundas in 1803. Fulton's claim is the first service that was commercially successful and lasting, and in the United States in particular it is often remembered as the beginning of the steamboat age. Engineers today say Fulton's real genius was in system design and business: choosing a reliable Boulton & Watt engine, sizing the boat for the Hudson's deep water, and having Livingston's legal monopoly and money behind him. That monopoly later became the centre of a famous US Supreme Court case, Gibbons v. Ogden (1824), which ruled that only the federal government could regulate trade between states, opening the rivers to competition. On the oceans, the key numbers were fuel and efficiency. Early marine engines worked at low pressure and burned several kilograms of coal for every horsepower each hour, which is why ships like Savannah could steam only a fraction of the way. Brunel's insight was about scaling: a ship's carrying capacity grows roughly with the cube of its size, while the water resistance it must overcome grows more slowly, roughly with the area of its hull. Later, compound and then triple-expansion engines (from the 1880s), using steam two or three times in cylinders of increasing size, cut coal use dramatically and made long voyages to Asia and Australia profitable. Finally, in the early 1900s, ships switched to steam turbines, which Part 17 explores.
funFact: The SS Savannah, the first ship to cross the Atlantic partly by steam in 1819, is the only ship known to have had paddle wheels that could be folded up and stored on deck.
